items.question: How much does it cost to hire you?
items.answer: Nothing upfront. We work on a contingency fee, which means our fee comes out of the recovery at the end. If there is no recovery, you owe us no attorney's fee.

items.question: How long do I have to bring a claim in New Jersey?
items.answer: In most New Jersey personal injury cases the deadline is two years from the date of the accident, and there are shorter notice deadlines when a public entity is involved. Waiting also makes evidence harder to obtain, so it is worth speaking to someone early even if you are unsure.

items.question: The insurance company already offered me money. Should I take it?
items.answer: Speak to a lawyer before you accept anything. Early offers usually arrive before the full extent of your injuries and treatment is known, and accepting one normally closes the claim for good.

items.question: What if the accident was partly my fault?
items.answer: New Jersey uses comparative negligence, so you can still recover as long as you were not more than 50% at fault — your recovery is reduced by your share. Do not assume you have no claim because you think you contributed.

items.question: Do I have to go to court?
items.answer: Most cases settle without a trial. We prepare every case as though it may be tried, because that is what gives a settlement negotiation weight, but the large majority resolve by agreement.

items.question: What if I don't have health insurance?
items.answer: In New Jersey your own auto policy's PIP coverage generally pays for accident-related medical treatment first, regardless of who caused the crash. We will help you work out what coverage applies.

sections.heading: Hurt at work in New Jersey? You have rights your employer may not explain.
sections.subheading: Workers' compensation should cover your medical treatment and part of your lost wages, whoever was at fault. But claims get delayed, treatment gets denied, and people get pushed back to work before they're ready. We make the system work the way it is supposed to.

sections.heading: Most workers' comp problems are avoidable — if you act early
sections.description: The insurance carrier chooses your doctor, decides what treatment is authorised, and decides when you are fit to return. Those decisions are challengeable, and they are far easier to challenge before they harden.

items.title: Treatment denied or cut off
items.description: If the carrier stops authorising the treatment your doctor recommends, that decision can be taken to a judge of compensation. You do not have to simply accept it.

items.title: Permanent disability, undervalued
items.description: Many injured workers settle without ever being assessed for permanent partial disability. That assessment is often the largest part of the claim.

items.title: Told you don't have a claim
items.description: Pre-existing conditions, repetitive strain injuries and injuries that developed over time are all potentially compensable in New Jersey. Being told otherwise is not the end of it.

items.title: A third party may also be liable
items.description: If a contractor, equipment manufacturer or driver caused your workplace injury, you may have a claim beyond workers' comp — one that can include pain and suffering.

items.title: Pushed back too early
items.description: Returning to full duty before you are ready risks re-injury and weakens your claim. We push back on premature return-to-work determinations.

items.title: Deadlines you may not know about
items.description: New Jersey requires notice to your employer promptly and a formal claim petition within two years. Missing these can end an otherwise good claim.

items.question: Can I be fired for filing a workers' comp claim?
items.answer: New Jersey law prohibits retaliating against an employee for filing a workers' compensation claim. If it happens, that is a separate claim in itself. Fear of retaliation is one of the most common reasons people do not claim what they are owed.

items.question: What if my employer says the injury wasn't their fault?
items.answer: Workers' compensation is a no-fault system. You generally do not need to prove your employer did anything wrong — only that the injury arose out of and in the course of your employment.

items.question: Can I use my own doctor?
items.answer: In New Jersey the employer or its insurance carrier generally has the right to direct authorised treatment. That does not mean their decisions are final — a judge can order treatment the carrier has refused.

items.question: What if the injury built up over time?
items.answer: Repetitive stress and occupational exposure injuries can be compensable in New Jersey. There does not have to be a single accident on a single day.

items.question: How much does a workers' comp attorney cost?
items.answer: Attorney fees in New Jersey workers' compensation cases are set and approved by the judge of compensation, and come out of the award. There is nothing to pay upfront.

items.question: Can I claim workers' comp and sue someone as well?
items.answer: Sometimes. You generally cannot sue your employer, but if a third party — a contractor, a driver, an equipment manufacturer — contributed to your injury, you may have a separate claim against them.
